south-dakota.agency_name: South Dakota Department of Health, Vital Records Office
south-dakota.birth_certificate: Not available for gender identity. The South Dakota Department of Health, Vital Records Office, handles birth-certificate amendments, but under ARSD 44:09:05:02, as interpreted in Nielsen (March 4, 2026), only data that was incorrect when the record was created can be corrected. A correctly recorded sex at birth cannot be changed to reflect gender identity, even with a court order. The general amendment fee listed by the Department of Health is $8 for amending a record one year or more after the event, plus $15 for a certified copy, but that fee does not create a gender-marker route.
south-dakota.court_order_required: No — a court order no longer enables a gender-marker change in South Dakota; the Supreme Court held in March 2026 that a court order cannot direct Vital Records to amend the sex designation to reflect gender identity.
south-dakota.drivers_license: Effectively unavailable as of July 2026. The South Dakota Department of Public Safety (DPS) previously allowed a change with a court order certifying the gender change or a signed affidavit from a licensed physician certifying that the applicant's gender had been medically altered, or under a later written policy a physician letter stating the applicant was undergoing gender-reassignment care. After HB 1184 took effect July 1, 2026, DPS has required an amended birth certificate, which South Dakota no longer issues for gender identity, so most applicants cannot complete the change. No X marker is available; only M and F.
south-dakota.marker_overview: South Dakota now effectively bans gender-marker changes. The South Dakota Supreme Court ruled on March 4, 2026 (Nielsen v. South Dakota, 2026 S.D. 12) that a birth certificate cannot be amended to reflect gender identity, and HB 1184, effective July 1, 2026, defines sex by reproductive biology throughout state law. The Department of Public Safety now requires an amended birth certificate for a driver's license change, which the state no longer issues for this purpose, creating a de facto ban there as well. Only M and F markers are offered; no X marker is available.
south-dakota.surgery_required: No — no surgery was required under the former driver's license route, which needed only a physician letter stating the applicant was undergoing gender-reassignment care or a court order, but that route is now effectively closed and no surgery can unlock a change.

tennessee.agency_name: Tennessee Department of Health, Office of Vital Records
tennessee.birth_certificate: Not available. The Tennessee Department of Health, Office of Vital Records, does not amend the sex designation on a birth certificate. Tenn. Code Ann. section 68-3-203(d) provides that the sex of an individual will not be changed on the original certificate of birth as a result of sex change surgery. The Sixth Circuit upheld this refusal in Gore v. Lee in July 2024. Name changes by court order are still processed separately, but they do not change the sex designation.
tennessee.court_order_required: No — a court order does not enable a gender-marker change in Tennessee; it is needed only for a legal name change, which is a separate process.
tennessee.drivers_license: Not available. The Tennessee Department of Safety and Homeland Security will not accept a request to change the sex designator on a driver's license or state ID to one inconsistent with the applicant's birth certificate, under Tenn. Code Ann. section 1-3-105(c), which defines sex as immutable biological sex as determined by anatomy and genetics existing at birth. The former physician-statement route in Rule 1340-01-13-.12(6) was nullified by a department declaratory order in March 2025. Litigation challenging the license policy remains pending. No X marker is available; only M and F.
tennessee.legal_aid_name: Legal Aid Society of Middle Tennessee and the Cumberlands
tennessee.marker_overview: Tennessee bans gender-marker changes on both state documents and is one of the most restrictive states in the country. Tennessee law has long barred changing the sex designation on a birth certificate, and since 2023 the Department of Safety and Homeland Security has refused driver's license sex-designation changes that do not match the birth certificate. A 2026 law (Public Chapter 938, effective May 7, 2026) further requires state and local entities to use the statutory biological-sex definition. Only M and F markers are offered; no X marker is available.
tennessee.surgery_required: No — surgery is not the barrier and cannot unlock a change; Tennessee bans the change outright, and the statute expressly says sex will not be changed on a birth certificate as a result of sex change surgery.

texas.agency_name: Texas Department of State Health Services, Vital Statistics Unit
texas.birth_certificate: Not available for gender identity. DSHS Vital Statistics will issue a new birth certificate based on sex only where the sex recorded at birth is proved by satisfactory evidence, such as medical records, to have been incomplete or inaccurate at birth. The correction application is Form VS-170, with a $25 filing fee for a new birth certificate based on the child's sex, but DSHS will not process an order that changes both name and sex, so a name-only court order should be used for a name change. Court orders directing a gender-marker change are not accepted for this purpose.
texas.court_order_required: No — a court order does not enable a gender-marker change in Texas; DPS and DSHS do not accept gender-marker court orders, and a court order is needed only for a legal name change, which must be in a separate name-only order.
texas.drivers_license: Not available except to correct a clerical error. DPS stopped processing gender-marker updates on driver's licenses and state IDs on August 20, 2024, even when presented with a court order, and will refuse a combined name-and-gender court order entirely, including for the name change in that order; a separate name-only court order is needed to update a name. First-time applicants are assigned the marker shown on their primary document, such as a birth certificate or passport. No X marker is available.
texas.marker_overview: Texas now bans gender-marker changes on both state documents for gender identity. Since August 20, 2024, the Texas Department of Public Safety (DPS) has stopped updating the sex marker on driver's licenses and state IDs, and since around August 30, 2024, the Department of State Health Services (DSHS) Vital Statistics Unit has stopped amending the sex marker on birth certificates. HB 229, effective September 1, 2025, defines male, female, man, and woman in state law, and most Texas judges have since stopped signing gender-marker orders. Only M and F markers are offered; no X marker is available.
texas.surgery_required: No — no surgery or medical procedure can unlock a gender-marker change in Texas; the only exception is proving with medical records that the sex recorded at birth was incomplete or inaccurate, which is a correction of an error, not a change to reflect gender identity.

utah.agency_name: Utah Office of Vital Records and Statistics
utah.birth_certificate: Apply to the Utah Office of Vital Records and Statistics with a certified copy of the court order for a sex designation change under Utah Code section 26B-8-111, plus a completed birth certificate request form and the applicable fees. The court petition must include evidence of medical history, care, or treatment related to transition, such as a letter signed by a licensed medical provider, and proof of six months of consistent outward expression as the requested sex. The statute, effective May 7, 2025, also requires findings that the person is not seeking the change to commit a crime, avoid creditors, or interfere with others' rights. A court-ordered amendment is filed with the Office of Vital Records and Statistics; the office states amendments generally take 6 to 12 weeks.
utah.court_order_required: Yes — a court order is required for a birth-certificate sex designation change, and in practice also for a driver's license change, since the Driver License Division requires a passport or birth certificate bearing the new gender.
utah.drivers_license: Update through the Utah Driver License Division by presenting a passport or birth certificate bearing the new gender, or a court order certifying the change. In practice this means obtaining the amended Utah birth certificate or a passport with the corrected marker first. Only M and F designations are available on a Utah license or ID; there is no X option.
utah.marker_overview: Utah allows a gender-marker change, but only by court order and only to M or F. A person must petition the district court under Utah Code section 26B-8-111 and prove, by clear and convincing evidence, that they have transitioned, have outwardly expressed the requested sex consistently for at least six months, and suffer clinically significant distress or impairment because of the sex on the birth certificate. Once the court grants the order, it is filed with the Office of Vital Records and Statistics for an amended birth certificate and can then be used with the Driver License Division. No X marker is available.
utah.surgery_required: No — Utah does not require surgery; the court must consider evidence of medical history, care, or treatment related to transition, such as a provider letter, and must find transition, six months of consistent outward expression, and clinically significant distress, but no specific surgery or procedure is required.

vermont.agency_name: Vermont Department of Health, Vital Records Office
vermont.birth_certificate: Mail an Application to Amend Birth Certificate, a notarized Affidavit of Gender Identity, and the current birth certificate to the Vermont Department of Health, Vital Records Office. No court order or medical documentation is required. A parent or guardian completes the affidavit for a registrant under 16. A new birth certificate is issued with no notation that a change was made, and records related to the change are confidential under 18 V.S.A. section 5112. A separate application and fee are required for a certified copy of the amended certificate; a name-change decree is included only if the name is also being changed.
vermont.court_order_required: No — no court order is needed for a gender-marker change on either document; a court order is needed only for a legal name change, which is a separate process.
vermont.drivers_license: Submit a Replacement License form to the Vermont Department of Motor Vehicles with the correct marker (M, F, or X) selected, in person, by mail, or online. Gender is a self-designated descriptor, so no medical documentation is required. A standard replacement license costs $24. An X marker is available on driver's licenses and state IDs.
vermont.marker_overview: Vermont has one of the simplest processes in the country, based on self-attestation with no court order and no medical proof. Since Act 88 in 2022, a person can change the gender marker on a Vermont birth certificate to M, F, or X with a notarized Affidavit of Gender Identity sent to the Department of Health, and can change the marker on a driver's license or state ID to M, F, or X by selecting it on the replacement license form, with no documentation required. All records related to a birth-certificate change are kept confidential.
vermont.surgery_required: No — no surgery, medical procedure, or doctor's letter is required for either document; Vermont removed the former physician-affidavit and court requirements in 2022 and now uses self-attestation.

virginia.agency_name: Virginia Department of Health, Division of Vital Records
virginia.birth_certificate: Submit to the Virginia Department of Health, Division of Vital Records: a request from the individual (or a parent if under 18), a copy of valid ID, a properly executed Changing Sex Designation form (VS42) with a live-ink signature and date from the treating health care provider stating the person has undergone clinically appropriate treatment for gender transition, and a certified copy of a court order changing the person's name only if the name is also being changed. The fee is $10 to establish the new birth certificate, plus $15 for each certified copy requested. Only M and F are available on a birth certificate; no X option is offered there.
virginia.court_order_required: No — no court order is needed for a gender-marker change on either document; a court order is needed only if the legal name is also being changed.
virginia.drivers_license: Change the sex designation through the Virginia Department of Motor Vehicles when applying for, renewing, or replacing a driver's license, learner's permit, identification card, or driver privilege card, or online if eligible. Select M, F, or X. Certification from a health care provider is not required. A certified court order is needed only if the name is also being changed.
virginia.marker_overview: Virginia splits the process by document: a driver's license or state ID marker can be changed by self-attestation with no medical proof, while a birth certificate requires a health care provider's form. The Department of Motor Vehicles allows M, F, or X on a license or ID, but a birth certificate change uses Form VS42, completed by a treating health care provider who certifies clinically appropriate treatment for gender transition. No court order is needed for a marker change alone.
virginia.surgery_required: No — no surgery is required; for a birth certificate a treating health care provider must certify clinically appropriate treatment for gender transition on Form VS42, with no specific procedure required, and for a driver's license no medical proof of any kind is required.

washington.agency_name: Washington State Department of Health, Center for Health Statistics
washington.birth_certificate: Submit a completed Request to Change Sex Designation on a Birth Certificate form to the Washington State Department of Health, Center for Health Statistics: Form DOH 422-143 for an adult or emancipated minor, or Form DOH 422-144 for a minor. An adult signs the form in front of a notary; no court order or physician letter is accepted or required for an adult. A minor's form is completed by a parent or legal guardian and requires a signed statement from a licensed health care provider. There is no fee to amend the record; a certified copy costs $25. The Department of Health states requests are currently processed in about three business days.
washington.court_order_required: No — no court order is needed for a gender-marker change on either document; a court order is needed only for a legal name change, which is a separate process.
washington.drivers_license: Submit a Change of Gender Designation Request form (Form 520-043) to the Washington Department of Licensing, in person at a licensing office or by mail, selecting M, F, or X and signing the form. No documentation from a doctor or a court is needed. If only the gender designation is changing and no photo change is needed, the replacement card is free by mail; a photo change requires an in-person visit and a replacement fee.
washington.marker_overview: Washington allows a gender-marker change to M, F, or X on both a birth certificate and a driver's license or state ID by self-attestation, with no court order and no medical proof for adults. The Department of Health handles birth certificates under WAC 246-490-075, and the Department of Licensing handles licenses and IDs. In 2026, SB 6081, signed March 16, 2026, added privacy protections restricting disclosure of sex-designation information and past changes in government records.
washington.surgery_required: No — no surgery, medical procedure, or doctor's letter is required for an adult on either document; a minor's birth-certificate change requires a licensed health care provider's statement, but no surgery is required.

west-virginia.agency_name: West Virginia Department of Health, Vital Registration
west-virginia.birth_certificate: Have a physician fill out the Sex Designation Form and provide the appropriate affidavit to the West Virginia Department of Health, Vital Registration office, with at least two items of documentary evidence supporting the facts. If documentary evidence cannot be obtained, the change may only be completed by petitioning a court and providing a certified copy of the court order. The amendment fee is $10, and each certified copy is $12. Older guidance also describes a court order for a gender change; the current Vital Registration instructions use the physician form and affidavit as the standard route, with a court order as the fallback. Only M and F are available; no X or nonbinary option.
west-virginia.court_order_required: No — a court order is not the usual route for either document; a physician-signed form is required for both, and a court order is the fallback for a birth certificate only if the required documentary evidence cannot be obtained.
west-virginia.drivers_license: Submit a completed Gender Designation Form (DMV-99-RO), signed by a licensed physician, to the West Virginia Division of Motor Vehicles. Under W. Va. Code R. section 91-4-9.5, any change of gender requires submission of the Gender Designation Form with certification by a medical doctor of the person's gender. Only M and F are available; no X marker is offered.
west-virginia.marker_overview: West Virginia still allows a gender-marker change to M or F, but only with a licensed physician's certification, and it does not recognize a nonbinary marker. A birth certificate is changed through the Vital Registration office with a physician-completed Sex Designation Form and affidavit, and a driver's license is changed through the Division of Motor Vehicles with a physician-signed Gender Designation Form. A 2024 law requires a birth certificate to list the child's sex at birth as male or female and bars the term non-binary, and 2025 legislation further limited recognition to male and female. A 2026 bill (HB 4171) that would further restrict changes was introduced only and is not law.
west-virginia.surgery_required: No — no surgery or sterilization is required; a licensed physician must complete and sign the Sex Designation or Gender Designation form certifying the person's gender, but the official sources do not require proof of surgery.

wisconsin.agency_name: Wisconsin Department of Health Services, State Vital Records Office
wisconsin.birth_certificate: Petition the circuit court for an order to change the name and sex on the birth certificate due to a surgical sex-change procedure under Wis. Stat. section 69.15(4); the court may not order a change on any other basis. Submit the certified court order, a Birth Certificate Request Form (F05291), and a notarized letter from the doctor who performed the surgery to the Wisconsin Department of Health Services, State Vital Records Office. The fee to file a sex-change court order is $20, and the first certified copy is $20. The certificate is marked amended unless the court orders a new certificate to be prepared.
wisconsin.court_order_required: Yes — a court order is required for a birth-certificate change; for a driver's license a court order is one accepted proof, the other being a physician's affidavit certifying the gender change.
wisconsin.drivers_license: Apply in person at a Wisconsin Department of Transportation Division of Motor Vehicles customer service center with a Driver's License Application (MV3001) and either an affidavit or statement from a licensed physician certifying the gender change or a court order for a gender change. Only M and F are offered; there is no X marker. A name change requires a separate court order and an updated Social Security record first.
wisconsin.marker_overview: Wisconsin is restrictive: a birth-certificate marker can be changed only by court order and only when the change is due to a surgical sex-change procedure, while a driver's license or state ID can be changed with either a court order or a physician's affidavit certifying the gender change. Only M and F markers are offered on both documents; no X marker is available. The birth-certificate rule has not changed in 2024-2026, but it remains one of the strictest in the country.
wisconsin.surgery_required: Yes — for a birth certificate, Wisconsin law permits a court to order the change only when it is due to a surgical sex-change procedure, supported by a doctor's letter about the surgery; a driver's license alone does not require surgery, only a physician affidavit or a court order.

wyoming.agency_name: Wyoming Department of Health, Vital Statistics Services
wyoming.birth_certificate: Not available for gender identity. Wyoming Vital Statistics Services, in the Wyoming Department of Health, now allows a change to the sex designation only to correct an error or omission in the sex recorded at birth, based on a signed statement from the hospital or attending physician where the birth occurred, or other acceptable evidence that an error occurred at birth. A court order reflecting a sex change is no longer accepted as the basis for the change under the amended Vital Records rule, Chapter 10, section 4(e). The general correction form lists a $30 fee for a correction from a court-ordered action and $20 for a correction not involving court action, but those fees do not create a gender-identity route. Litigation over the rule is pending before the Wyoming Supreme Court.
wyoming.court_order_required: No — a court order no longer enables a gender-marker change in Wyoming; since March 13, 2026, a court order reflecting a sex change is not accepted as the basis to amend a birth certificate, and a driver's license change now depends on that amended birth certificate.
wyoming.drivers_license: Effectively unavailable as of April 2, 2026. The Wyoming Department of Transportation previously allowed a change with a Gender Designation Change Request Form signed by the applicant and a physician, therapist, counselor, psychiatric social worker, or other medical or social service provider. It now requires an amended birth certificate as proof of a legal gender change, which Wyoming no longer issues for gender identity, so most applicants cannot complete the change. No X marker is available; only M and F.
wyoming.marker_overview: Wyoming now effectively bans gender-marker changes on both state documents. The Wyoming Department of Health issued an emergency rule on November 19, 2025, and made it permanent on March 13, 2026, so a court order reflecting a sex change is no longer a basis to amend the sex designation on a birth certificate. On April 2, 2026, the Wyoming Department of Transportation changed its driver's license policy to accept only an amended birth certificate as proof of a legal gender change, which the state no longer issues for this purpose. Only M and F markers are offered; no X marker is available.
wyoming.surgery_required: No — no surgery or medical proof can now unlock a change; the ban turns on the birth record, not on medical evidence, and only a correction of an error in the sex recorded at birth is allowed.
